welcome.title: Aurorapp - Northern Lights
welcome.message:
Aurorapp - Northern Lights is a modern, vibrant app designed for aurora hunters and curious travelers alike.
If you're interested in Northern Lights activity, this app is for you.

perception.title: What you see with the naked eye
perception.message:
First, it’s important to know that the Northern Lights rarely look like the spectacular photos you may have seen. When auroral activity is low, they often appear pale white to the naked eye.
That can be disappointing at first… but it’s normal. In reality, our eyes struggle to perceive colors in the dark, while camera sensors are far more sensitive.
During geomagnetic storms, you may see fast-moving, faint, slightly colored “curtains” in the sky. If you know what to look for, it can be truly breathtaking.

how.title: How does it work?
how.message:
The Northern Lights are a natural phenomenon originating from the Sun.
They occur when solar particles, carried by the solar wind, interact with Earth’s magnetic field. They are most common near the magnetic poles, in the auroral zone (roughly between 65° and 75° latitude), where they collide with the upper atmosphere (oxygen, hydrogen, ozone, and other gases). The energy released becomes visible as dancing lights.
This phenomenon typically occurs around 100 km altitude, near the Kármán line (often used as the boundary between the atmosphere and space), within the thermosphere (85–690 km).

For more technical and scientific information, here are a couple of resources:
  • visitnorway.fr
  • bastienfoucher.com

forecast.title: How can we predict it?
forecast.message:
Thanks to NASA satellites designed to study solar particles. These satellites are positioned at Lagrange Point 1, between Earth and the Sun, about 1,500,000 km away.
The data is processed by the Space Weather Prediction Center, a U.S.-based space weather service.
By combining multiple indicators (such as Bz, Kp, particle density, solar wind speed, and cloud cover), we can estimate visibility conditions. Two satellites are commonly referenced: ACE (Advanced Composition Explorer), nearing the end of its mission, and DSCOVR (Deep Space Climate Observatory), which is now the primary source.

capricious.title: How accurate are the forecasts?
capricious.message:
Not very.
Scientific data cannot guarantee aurora visibility 100% of the time. These indicators are best used to estimate probability and improve your understanding. Cloud cover and light pollution also play a major role.
The best approach is still to go outside and check the sky.

colors.title: Green, purple, or pink
colors.message:
Aurora colors depend on the altitude at which solar wind plasma interacts with atmospheric gases. The higher the particle density, the deeper particles can penetrate into the atmosphere.
  • Purple / Red: around 200–500 km altitude, electrons mainly excite helium and some oxygen (which is scarce at that altitude).
  • Green: around 100–200 km altitude, electrons excite oxygen, which is denser there. This is the most common color.
  • Pink: around 80–100 km altitude, electrons excite hydrogen and nitrogen. This is rarer and typically requires a dense and/or highly energetic solar wind.

where.title: Where can you see them?
where.message:
The closer you are to one of Earth’s poles, the higher your chances of seeing auroras.
Alaska, Northern Canada, Norway, Iceland, and Lapland are prime destinations after dusk. In the Southern Hemisphere, sightings are most common in New Zealand, due to the lack of land at lower latitudes. Of course, it also depends on solar activity.
In summer, it’s impossible to see auroras near the North Pole because of the midnight sun. You’ll need to get closer to the winter solstice (around December 21). Conversely, in summer it can still be possible to see auroras by moving closer to the South Pole.

corona.title: Aurora coronas
corona.message:
An aurora corona is an aurora that appears like a crown at the zenith (90° above your head). The aurora can look circular, almost like a spiral. The base is usually around 80–100 km altitude, while the top reaches much higher into the thermosphere. This perspective can make rays appear to converge, creating the “crown” effect.
You generally need high latitude and around Kp 5 to have a good chance of seeing one.

steve.title: STEVE
steve.message:
STEVE (Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement) is the name given to a new type of auroral phenomenon discovered in 2017 by aurora watchers in a Facebook group in Alberta, Canada.
It appears as a long, narrow purple ribbon across the sky. Scientists were initially unable to explain it. In 2018, research led by a professor at the University of Calgary described STEVE as a flow of hot gas (around 3000°) moving faster than the surrounding air, which gives it its purple glow.
The “STEVE phenomenon” can last up to an hour, moves at speeds up to 6 km/s, and can stretch up to 25 km. It has been observed in Alberta, around the latitude of Calgary.

legends.title: Myths & Legends
legends.message: Many legends about auroras exist, and they vary widely depending on the region. Here are a few examples.

alaska.message: Some Inuit feared the aurora, seeing it as the dancing souls of animals such as salmon, seals, beluga whales, or deer. They would carry knives to try to chase it away.

canada.message: Inuit from Hudson Bay believed the sky was a vast dome with holes through which the spirits of the dead passed on their way to the heavens. They would light torches to guide the newcomers. Some West Indian peoples saw them as friendly giants.

vikings.message: Vikings associated auroras with the Valkyries, messengers of the Norse god Odin. After each war, Odin selected the bravest warriors to join Valhalla for Ragnarök, and the Valkyries would come to retrieve them. Auroras were believed to be reflections of the Valkyries’ armor.

sami.message:
The Sámi people live across Northern Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia’s Kola Peninsula. For some tribes, auroras were bad omens associated with death, appearing after tragic events.
For others, they were a good omen, like the breath of whales in the Arctic Ocean.

finlande.message:
Legend says Arctic foxes created the aurora by running across the sky so fast that sparks flew from their tails. Another story tells of “fire foxes” swirling snow up into the sky, reflecting moonlight.
In Finnish, the Northern Lights are called “Revontulet”, which literally means “fire fox”.

france.message: Norman fishermen feared auroras because of their reddish color. Since auroras rarely reach France at such low latitudes, they were seen as a sign of misfortune.

romains.message: In Roman mythology, Aurora was the goddess of dawn. The word “borealis” refers to Boreas, the Greek god of the north wind. “Aurora Borealis” can therefore be interpreted as “dawn of the north wind”. In many languages, this phenomenon is simply called the “Northern Lights”.

legends.conclusion: These are only brief summaries—there are many more legends across Scandinavia, Russia, and North America, and they differ greatly. The one thing they all share is that auroras leave no one indifferent.

annecdotes.title: Fun facts
annecdotes.une: Galileo is said to have coined the term “Aurora Borealis” in 1619.
annecdotes.deux: Auroras have been observed on Mars, Venus, Saturn, Jupiter, and Uranus. Because Mercury is small and very close to the Sun, it has virtually no atmosphere—so auroras cannot occur there.
annecdotes.trois: In the Northern Hemisphere we have Aurora Borealis; in the Southern Hemisphere, Aurora Australis. “Polar aurora” refers to auroras at both poles.
annecdotes.quatre: Aurora Australis is relatively rare because there is little land near the South Pole. It can be seen from Antarctica, Tasmania, southern Australia, and the far south of New Zealand.
annecdotes.cinq: Auroras depend on the Sun’s magnetic activity, which follows an ~11-year cycle. At solar maximum, magnetic storms can be intense and produce spectacular auroras. They can also interfere with magnetic instruments such as compasses.
annecdotes.six: Two cities in Alaska—Fairbanks and Nome—can experience aurora visibility on more than 200 days per year.

kp.title: The Kp index
kp.message:
The K index (or planetary Kp index) measures the magnitude of geomagnetic storms. It is an excellent indicator of disturbances in Earth’s magnetic field, but it does not guarantee aurora visibility. Measurements are taken worldwide every 3 hours. The scale goes from 0 to 9:
  • Kp 0: Very calm, low visibility in far northern skies
  • Kp 1: Very calm (Yellowknife, Reykjavík, Fairbanks, Whitehorse)
  • Kp 2: Quiet, usually visible further north, faint (Anchorage, Edmonton, Saskatoon, Winnipeg, Trondheim)
  • Kp 3: Visible near zenith, pale green (Calgary, Ålesund)
  • Kp 4: Bright, steady, dynamic; some color appears (Vancouver, Minneapolis, Oslo, Helsinki, Stockholm)
  • Kp 5: Minor storm; bright and colorful; red/purple may appear; small chance of an aurora corona (Seattle, Chicago, Toronto, Halifax, Edinburgh)
  • Kp 6: Moderate storm; stronger than the previous level (Portland, Indianapolis, Dublin, Manchester, Moscow, Christchurch)
  • Kp 7: Strong storm; high chance of an aurora corona (Salt Lake City, Nashville, London, Brussels, Melbourne, Wellington)
  • Kp 8: Severe storm; auroras may be seen around 50° latitude (Paris, Munich, San Francisco, Las Vegas, Atlanta)
  • Kp 9: Extreme storm; auroras may be seen around 40° latitude (Barcelona, Marseille, Rome, Miami). Auroras can appear red. This is rare and typically requires a powerful coronal mass ejection.

solarWind.title: Solar wind
solarWind.message:
Solar wind is plasma (a gas made mostly of electrons, ions, and protons). There are two main types:
  • slow (around 300 km/s)
  • fast (between 500 and 800 km/s)
The fast wind has the most direct impact on Earth and varies with solar activity and cycles.
Solar wind is emitted continuously, but events such as coronal holes or solar flares can increase its speed and density.
The faster the wind, the more dynamic auroras can be. The higher the density, the stronger they can become. However, solar wind doesn’t act alone—it is closely linked to the Interplanetary Magnetic Field (IMF).

cmi.title: Interplanetary Magnetic Field (IMF)
cmi.message:
The IMF provides values such as Bt and the Bx, By, Bz components.
These components are vectors that define directions relative to Earth. For auroral activity, Bt and Bz are the most important.
  • Bz: an axis passing through Earth’s north and south poles. When Bz is southward (negative), it can couple with Earth’s magnetosphere (which is generally northward), allowing solar wind particles to enter more easily and increasing auroral activity. Bz is often considered in the range -15 to 15.
  • Bt: represents the strength of the IMF. The higher the value, the more favorable conditions can be for geomagnetic storms. As a rough guide, ~15 nT is moderate, and ~25 nT is strong.
When the solar cycle is at minimum, the Sun’s magnetic field is closer in strength to Earth’s. At solar maximum, many sunspots appear and the Sun’s magnetic field becomes much more complex.
Solar wind then carries these magnetic disturbances toward Earth.

solarCycle.title: Solar cycle
solarCycle.message:
The solar cycle is largely tracked using the number of sunspots visible on the Sun’s surface. Sunspots are darker, cooler regions and are closely linked to solar flares and storms that can impact Earth. The cycle peaks roughly every 11.2 years on average.
This pattern was identified thanks to early observations, including Galileo’s work in the 17th century. Recorded solar cycle data goes back mainly to the 18th century, allowing scientists to study highs and lows over time.
Solar activity can also be measured using the 10.7 cm solar flux, a more precise index based on radio emissions at 2800 MHz (wavelength 10.7 cm).

help.title: Tutorial: How does Aurorapp work?
help.message:
It’s very simple!
  1. When you launch Aurorapp for the first time, it uses your current location, so the app starts with your initial position.
  2. You can change the location anytime from the world map in the “Auroras” tab.
  3. Then check solar activity in the “Auroras” tab and cloud cover in the “Weather” tab.
  4. Finally, it helps to understand how auroras, solar wind, and the Kp index work. You can use Aurorapp’s documentation in the “Learn more” section, or the Internet.

    5. Reminder: these data points are indicators for aurora hunting. They do not guarantee you will see auroras 100% of the time.

noSwpcData.title: Data no longer displayed
noSwpcData.message: Solar wind or Kp data not showing / stuck loading? This is most likely because NOAA SWPC is experiencing an issue. Please be patient—it usually only lasts a few minutes. It’s very common, so there’s no need to worry.

art2.title: Article 2: Access and use
art2.text:
Users can access the application at any time, from anywhere.
An internet connection is required to access most features of the application.
The application provides information related to the Northern Lights. Thanks to geolocation, users can view data from the Space Weather Prediction Center (United States), processed and formatted by the developer. Users can also view weather information for the selected city.
The application contains no advertising and is entirely free. It does not generate any revenue.

art3.title: Article 3: Personal data
art3.text:
In accordance with data protection laws, users have the right to access, rectify, delete, and object to the processing of their personal data.
As a result:
  • Only the user’s geolocation data is requested to ensure proper operation of the application on their smartphone/tablet. This data is stored locally on the device using “Local Storage”.
  • Geolocation data is only created when requested by the user. The application does not track the user’s movements.
  • No information is collected, transmitted, used, or processed by the developer at this time.
  • No cookies are used in this application.
  • No personal or non-personal data is stored anywhere other than on the user’s device.
  • No database has been set up for this application.
  • There are currently no plans to change how this data is managed over time.

art4.title: Article 4: Intellectual property
art4.text:
Logos and graphic design are protected by intellectual property laws, in particular copyright. Users are asked to contact the developer before reusing them.
Credits are available in the “Settings” tab for any related information. Any content not listed in the credits belongs to the developer.
